THE REGNIER STRADIVARI. A Highly Important Violin by Antonio Stradivari, Cremona 1727, bearing the original label Antonius Stradiuarius Cremonensis faciebat Anno 1727, the handsome two-piece back of narrow horizontal curl of Italian growth, the ribs and head of similar wood, the table of medium grain in the centre opening out very slightly towards the flanks, the varnish of a rich orange-brown colour, length of back 13 15/16in. (354mm.), in mahogany-veneered case by W. E. Hill & Sons, with outer canvas cover (3) Certificates and Letters: A certificate from Hart & Sons (signed by George Hart) dated 26th July 1897 and annotated by John Audley Harvey on 17th May 1915 and Robert A. Bauer on 11th October 1915; A receipt from Robert Bauer to Jules Fuerst dated 11th October 1915 and a telegram of the same date; A letter from Kalman Ronay to Jules Fuerst dated 27th October 1915 formally acknowledging the loan of the instrument to him; A certificate from W. E. Hill & Sons, London dated 16th January 1929. Literature: W. Henry, Arthur F. & Alfred E. Hill, Antonio Stradivari, His life and works, 1st Ed., p. 81 (referred to under the date 1726); Ernest N. Doring, How many Strads, our heritage from the Master, p. 280; Herbert K. Goodkind, Violin Iconography of Antonio Stradivari, p. 736; William Henley, Antonio Stradivari and his Instruments, p. 79; The Strad, June 1938. Provenance: Leon Reynier or Regnier (see footnote below); Hart & Son; Captain John Audley Harvey; Robert A. Bauer; Jules Fuerst.  This violin is referred to by Doring and Henley as the “ex Regnier or Reynier”. The confusion over the name seems to stem from the Hart certificate in which George Hart states that “The violin is known as ‘the Regnier Stradivari’ from its having belonged to the celebrated French violinist of that name.” In fact he was probably referring to Leon Reynier who is known to have been a prize winner at the Paris Conservatoire in 1847 and who, up until 1871 owned another Stradivari violin dated 1681 which has taken his name (see Doring p. 43). According to Hart the present violin was purchased by them from an un-named English gentleman who had previously purchased it from the widow of ‘M. Regnier’. Hart sold the instrument to Captain John Audley Harvey in 1897. In 1915 it passed briefly into the ownership of Robert Bauer who within six months had sold it to Jules Fuerst. The Hill certificate, made out to Madame Fuerst, describes the violin as a fine and characteristic example of its period (See Colour Plates)
